newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones index ends lower after soaring 100 points.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones index ends lower after soaring 100 points.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average ended lower Tuesday after a rally of more than 100 points sparked by good news on inflation unravelled in the last hour of the session on profit-taking.
The Dow ended down 4.61 points at 6,656.08. The blue-chip index has now fallen for five straight sessions, the first time it has done so since last June.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,399 to 1,030 on heavy volume of 526 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The stock market tracked the volatile session in bonds, where a rally of more than a full point in the Treasury's key 30-year bond also lost steam.

At the close, the long-bond held a small gain of 6/32, which trimmed its yield to 6.93 percent from 6.94 percent on Monday. Early in the session, the yield, which moves in the opposite direction of the bond's price, hovered at 6.83 percent.

Financial markets exploded from the start on news that the Employment Cost Index -- a key indicator of wage price pressure -- rose 0.8 percent in the last three months of 1996, slightly less than the 0.9 percent that Wall Street had expected, quashing fears of a dangerous inflationary spike.
The Labour Department reported that U.S. workers' compensation in the fourth quarter rose 0.8 percent after a 0.6 percent gain in the third quarter.
"The ECI started the day off well and said there is no current danger of inflation even with the unemployment rate as low as it is," said Stan Shipley, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
Later, however, strong retail sales and consumer confidence data eroded the bond market's rally and triggered stiff profit-taking in stocks.

"The ECI was a good excuse for a bounce and there was a lot of short covering going on early," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "But when people saw the market up 100 points and (bond) yields starting to work back up towards 7 percent, the bounce got sold."
Analysts said the stock market's failure to hold onto its gains indicated further headway was unlikely soon.
"I read it as an indication of subsiding momentum," said Eugene Peroni, chief technical analyst at Janney, Montgomery Scott. "We expect the market will probably show some expansive swings here."

Some stocks were able to overcome the late selling, with one particularly notable example being International Business Machines Corp., which broke a four session losing streak by jumping 4-1/4 to 150.
IBM declared a two-for-one stock split and benefitted from a upgrade by Salomon Brothers analyst John Jones, who now rates the world's laregst computer maker a strong buy.

Drug shares were also strong after several companies reported better than expected earnings. Merck & Co. Inc. climbed 2-1/2 to 87 and Eli Lilly & Co., which reported on Monday, gained 1-7/8 to 82-1/4.

ITT Corp. soared 14-1/8 to 56-3/4 in the first trading since the company received a $55 per share, $6.5 billion hostile bid after Monday's market close from Hilton Hotels Corp. Analysts said Hilton would probably have to raise its offer to complete the deal.
Shares in Hilton rose 2-1/2 to 27-3/4.

Federal National Mortgage Association climbed 1-3/4 to 38-3/4. The company, which is the nation's largest source of funds for home mortgages, said it exceeded all its housing goals set by regulators in 1996.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 1.56 points to 1,354.37.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was unchanged at 765.02. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.91 to 588.07.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 0.08 to 402.86. The average share was up 1 cent.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,414.928 up 1.605 or 0.02 percent.
